newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-SPRINT KING BAILEY LOOKS TO MAKE MORE HISTORY.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-SPRINT KING BAILEY LOOKS TO MAKE MORE HISTORY.

text.p: If Pele was born to play soccer and Muhammad Ali was born to box, then Olympic sprint champion Donovan Bailey was born to run. But for the first 23 years of his life it seems someone forgot to tell him.

Instead he concentrated on making fast moves in other directions. Clearly a man in a hurry, he was so successful in business he bought a Porsche when he was just 21. He ran a profitable marketing company with his brother and owned his own house.

In the late 1980s, when Canada was reeling from Ben Johnson's doping scandal at the Seoul Olympics, it never occured to Bailey that he was destined to bring the dignity back to his adopted homeland which Johnson's drug-fuelled victory in the 100 metres final had destroyed.

While Johnson, his coach Charlie Francis and other athletes were revealing the extent of their steroid abuse in public, Bailey, who like Johnson was born in Jamaica and moved to Canada as a youngster, was getting into arguments at college basketball games.
"I fell in love with basketball," he said. "And after leaving school in 1985 carried on playing the game as a weekend warrior."

Athletics did not figure greatly in the teenaged Bailey's life, although he had run an impressive 10.65 seconds for the 100 metres when he was just 16, two years later he could only register a best time of 11.37 seconds.
It was to be seven years before athletics made any impact on his life again. Or rather, before he had an impact on athletics.

One turning point came while he was at York University and took part in an indoor 60 metres. Twenty-three years old and without a single training session, he clocked 6.70 seconds to the astonishment of everyone who saw it.

Gradually athletics began to have an appeal, but his progress between 1991 and 1993 was consistent but not spectacular. He was 23 when he first broke 11 seconds and only reached world class at the age of 26 in 1994 when he ran 10.03.
The moment that helped change Bailey from an also- ran to world number one happened at the 1993 world championships in Stuttgart.
Bailey was accosted by American coach Dan Pfaff who said to him: "You are a mess, but you have the tools to become the fastest man in the world. If you trust me, I can help you do it."
Within two years of that meeting Bailey won the world title in Gothenburg in 9.97 seconds. A year ago in Atlanta he won the Olympic title in a world record of 9.84.

Now just two months short of his 30th birthday, he arrived in Athens on Sunday for the world championships complaining of a virus and still troubled by a niggling hamstring injury -- but promising to run faster than ever this summer.

"I know I can go a lot faster than my world record, and if I put together the perfect race -- something I have never done yet -- I think you're talking about a major improvement in the world record. I think we're talking about 9.7 seconds. Maybe even below 9.7 you never know."

Bailey has not been in the greatest form so far this, but has already made headlines for his victory over Michael Johnson in their ill-fated 150 metres head-to-head in Toronto's Skydome in May which earned Bailey $1.5 million after Johnson failed to finish the race.
That was a circus. This is the real thing. If he equals his Atlanta feat of a a world-record victory in the 100, he will pick up a bonus of $160,000, but he will not have things all his own way.
Ato Boldon of Trinidad, Americans Maurice Greene, Jon Drummond and Tim Montgomery and Namibian Frankie Fredericks have all run faster than Bailey this season.
Sunday's 100 final promises to be one of the highlights of the championship. And even if Bailey should lose, one thing is certain.
He would no longer be world champion, but never again will he be an also-ran.
